high.title: intent:// URL launched without clearing its component and selector
high.description: Intent.parseUri() turns a URL into an Intent that is then started, and this file does not call both setComponent(null) and setSelector(null) on it. The application is vulnerable to Intent Redirection via the `intent://` scheme. In `getUrlOverrideSettings`, the app uses `Intent.parseUri()` to convert a URL into an Intent and then calls `startActivity()` on that Intent. Before starting the activity, the app attaches a sensitive extra (`intent.putExtra("info", "Sensitive information")`). An attacker can host a webpage that redirects the WebView to an `intent://` URI specifying a component under the attacker's control; the application will then start that component and leak the sensitive information contained in the 'info' extra to the attacker's app.
high.impact: A web page or link that reaches this code names any activity in the app - exported or not - with extras of its choosing, the classic WebView-to-private-component jump.

lines_html: if (!url.contains("intent")) {
android.content.Intent intent = android.content.Intent.parseUri(url, 1);
intent.putExtra("info", "Sensitive information");
android.util.Log.d(TAG, "intent action = " + intent.getAction());
webView.getContext().startActivity(intent);

high.recommendation: After parseUri(), call setComponent(null), setSelector(null) and addCategory(BROWSABLE), or launch only intents whose target is on an allowlist.

low.title: Exported activity DisplayActivity has no permission protection
low.description: Activity "edu.ksu.cs.benign.DisplayActivity" is reachable by any app on the device (Has an intent-filter and no explicit android:exported (implicitly exported)) and declares no permission. It handles DISP. Deep-link schemes: benign. The DisplayActivity is exported and contains an intent-filter that makes it reachable via the 'benign://ghera/' URI. There is no permission requirement to launch this activity, allowing any third-party app on the device to invoke it and potentially manipulate the displayed text via the 'info' extra.
low.impact: Unauthorized access to an app component, though the current impact is limited to UI manipulation.
low.recommendation: Set android:exported="false" if it is internal, or guard it with a signature-level permission and validate all input.

reasons: The gain is limited to UI manipulation, which is a low-impact result for an exported component.

info.description: android:debuggable="true" lets any user with adb attach a debugger to the process, read and modify memory, and inspect application data. The android:debuggable attribute is set to true in the manifest. This allows an attacker with ADB access to attach a debugger to the process, inspect memory, and execute arbitrary code via the JDWP protocol.

reasons: Debuggable release build. A debuggable build is a release-pipeline defect rather than an exploitable flaw - attaching a debugger already requires ADB access to the device. Worth fixing, not worth a severity.

info.title: Missing screenshot protection (FLAG_SECURE)
info.description: The application does not set the FLAG_SECURE window flag in any of its activities. This allows the system and other apps (with appropriate permissions) to take screenshots or record the screen, including potential sensitive data shown in DisplayActivity.
info.impact: Sensitive information displayed on the screen can be captured without the user's knowledge.
info.recommendation: Call getWindow().setFlags(WindowManager.LayoutParams.FLAG_SECURE, WindowManager.LayoutParams.FLAG_SECURE) in activities that handle sensitive data.

reasons: Screen contents not protected from capture. Without FLAG_SECURE, what a screen shows can end up in screenshots, screen recordings and the task-switcher preview. That matters on screens showing credentials, card numbers or balances; on its own it is a hardening note.
Screen contents not protected from capture reaches at most CVSS 3.3 (Low); the vector given scores this finding above anything the class does.

info.title: No network security config declared
info.description: The app declares neither android:networkSecurityConfig nor usesCleartextTraffic, so it relies on platform defaults and pins no domain. With targetSdkVersion 27 those defaults still permit cleartext HTTP (see the cleartext finding).
info.impact: Without pinning, anyone who gets a CA trusted on the device can read and alter the app's TLS traffic.
info.recommendation: Declare a network security config that disables cleartext and pins the domains that carry sensitive traffic.

reasons: No certificate pinning. Pinning defends against an attacker who already controls a trusted CA or the device's trust store. Without one of those, TLS is still doing its job. It becomes a finding when paired with what the unpinned channel actually carries.
Lack of pinning is a hardening step and only matters if the channel carries sensitive data.

info.title: targetSdkVersion 27 permits cleartext traffic by default
info.description: targetSdk 27 predates API 28, where cleartext HTTP became opt-in. The app targets SDK version 27 and does not define a Network Security Configuration. On this SDK level, cleartext HTTP traffic is permitted by default, making network communication susceptible to interception and man-in-the-middle (MITM) attacks.
info.impact: Exposure of sensitive data transmitted over unencrypted HTTP channels.

reasons: Cleartext permitted by configuration. The flag permits HTTP; it does not show that anything is sent over it. Name a request that actually goes out in cleartext, and what it carries, and this is a genuine finding.
Permitting cleartext traffic is a configuration state; it requires a specific HTTP request to be a vulnerability.
warnings: Cleartext is blocked by default from targetSdk 28; confirm the declared target and any network security config.

info.title: Task hijacking (StrandHogg) possible on Android 10 and lower
info.description: minSdkVersion 22 lets the app run on Android versions before 11, and its task affinity is its package name "edu.ksu.cs.benign". There, another app can declare the same affinity, with allowTaskReparenting, and have its own activity shown in this app's task. The app targets SDK 27 (Android 8.1). In versions of Android 10 and below, apps can be vulnerable to task hijacking (StrandHogg) if they use certain launch modes and affinities, allowing a malicious app to place its own activities on top of the victim app's task.
info.impact: An attacker can present a fake UI to the user to phish credentials or intercept interactions.
info.recommendation: Raise minSdkVersion to 30, where Android fixed this. Until then, android:taskAffinity="" on the <application> mitigates the original attack, though not its runtime variant on unpatched Android 9 and lower.
